summary: Defines a MIB module for managing the Transmission Control Protocol over IPv6, as part of a series of IPv6 MIB documents. It is now historic and was replaced by RFC 4022 and RFC 8096.

eli5.summary: These are the dials and counters that let a network manager watch TCP connections over the new internet addresses. Newer documents replaced them.

subtitle: Tracking TCP connections over the new internet addresses

tldr.problem: TCP connections over IPv6 need to be monitored and managed, but the existing TCP management objects were designed for IPv4 and cannot represent IPv6 addresses.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC defines a new MIB table specifically for TCP connections between IPv6 endpoints, following the pattern of existing IPv4 TCP management but using IPv6 address representation.
tldr.outcome: Network managers can now monitor and control TCP connections over IPv6 using standard SNMP management tools, though this RFC is now historic and replaced by RFC 4022 and RFC 8096.

today: RFC 2452 is Historic. It was replaced by RFC 4022 and RFC 8096, which provide updated MIB definitions for TCP and IPv6 in the modern SNMP framework.

sections.title: Introduction to Network Management
sections.content:
Network managers need to watch how the network is working: what computers are talking to each other, how much data is flowing, and whether anything is broken. To do this, they use a system called SNMP (Simple Network Management Protocol) that lets them read and adjust dials and counters on network devices.

A Management Information Base (MIB) is a collection of these dials and counters. When a new protocol or feature comes out, network managers need a new set of counters to watch it.
sections.eli5: Think of a dashboard in a car: the manager needs dials to see how fast the car is going, how hot the engine is, and so on. When you get a new kind of car, you need new dials.

sections.title: Why TCP Needs New Management Objects
sections.content:
TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) itself is transparent to which version of IP carries it. A TCP connection works the same way whether it uses IPv4 or IPv6: it still tracks open connections, counts packets, and manages timeouts.

However, TCP connections need to record addresses: the source address and the destination address. The old MIB objects used a data type called IpAddress, which can only hold a 32-bit IPv4 address. IPv6 addresses are 128 bits, so they cannot fit in that old format.
sections.eli5: TCP itself does not care if addresses are old-style or new-style. But the notebook for writing down addresses was designed for short old-style addresses. New-style addresses are too long to fit on the page.

sections.title: The IPv6 TCP Connection Table
sections.content:
Rather than redefine the entire TCP MIB, this RFC adds a separate table called ipv6TcpConnTable that holds only TCP connections between IPv6 endpoints. IPv4 TCP connections continue to be tracked in the existing table.

Each row in the new table tracks one TCP connection and records the local IPv6 address, the local port, the remote IPv6 address, the remote port, and the connection state (listen, established, closing, and so on). An additional index field helps identify which network interface the connection uses, since IPv6 link-local addresses may not be unique across interfaces.

The table shows the TCP connection states defined in RFC 793: closed, listen, syn-sent, syn-received, established, fin-wait-1, fin-wait-2, close-wait, last-ack, closing, and time-wait.
sections.eli5: Instead of rewriting the whole notebook, we add a new page just for new-style addresses. Each line on the page describes one conversation: who started it, who is on the other end, and what state it is in.

sections.title: Managing TCP Connections
sections.content:
The MIB includes one object that network managers can change: the connection state. A manager can set the state to deleteTCB, which terminates the connection by deleting its TCP Control Block on the managed device. This allows remote management of connections without logging into the device directly.

The RFC recommends that devices return an error if a manager tries to set the state to anything other than the delete command, to prevent accidental damage to live connections.
sections.eli5: The manager can flip one switch: the switch that ends a conversation. All the other information is just for watching, not changing.

sections.title: Security and Privacy
sections.content:
The ability to delete TCP connections is powerful: if an attacker can change this object, they can disrupt all network traffic. Additionally, the list of active TCP connections reveals which services are running and who is talking to whom. This information could help an attacker plan denial-of-service attacks or target specific services.

The RFC recommends using SNMPv3 with the User-based Security Model and View-based Access Control to protect access to these objects. Only authorized users should be able to read the list of connections or delete them. Not all SNMP versions provide encryption, so administrators should choose versions carefully.
sections.eli5: Knowing all the conversations happening tells an attacker what is important to break. You need a strong lock on this notebook so only trusted people can look at it or change it.
